title: NBIC R Stamp Audit Support: NDE Side of the R Review
description: Ready the NDE side of your National Board R certificate review: NBIC Part 3 manual, NDE procedures, subcontractors and R-1/R-2 records. Contact us today.
h1: NBIC R-Stamp Audit Support: Preparing the NDE Side of Your National Board R Certificate Review
html:
This page is for quality managers at boiler repair shops, vessel repair firms, field service contractors and owner-users who hold, or are applying for, a National Board "R" Certificate of Authorization, and for the NDE companies that examine their repairs. Atlantis NDT gives these organizations ASNT NDT Level III support on the nondestructive examination side of the R program: the NDE wording in the NBIC Part 3 quality manual, the procedures and personnel files behind it, and the control of NDE subcontractors that the review team will test. Request R-stamp audit support and we reply within one business day.

The R certificate in plain terms

The National Board Inspection Code (NBIC, also called NB-23) is published by the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors. The current edition is 2025, issued in four parts: Part 1 Installation, Part 2 Inspection, Part 3 Repairs and Alterations, and Part 4 Pressure Relief Devices. The National Board publishes a new edition every two years, and each edition becomes mandatory six months after its issue date.

Part 3 is the one that matters here. The R certificate and its R symbol stamp authorize an organization to repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items after they have left the original manufacturer. A repair restores an item to a safe and satisfactory condition; an alteration changes something the original design relied on, such as adding a nozzle, re-rating pressure or temperature, or changing a dimension that affects strength. The distinction drives the paperwork, the design review and the NDE, and our NB-23 explainer walks through where the line falls.

NBIC has no force of its own. It becomes law where a state, city or province adopts it, and the jurisdiction decides which items fall under it. Scope on an R certificate is defined by activity (repairs, alterations, and engineered repairs and alterations), by location (shop, field, or both) and by material (metallic or non-metallic). Engineered repairs and alterations follow NBIC Part 3, Supplement 11.

How the R review is run

The National Board's procedure for accrediting repair organizations is NB-415, currently Revision 8, approved by its Board of Trustees in May 2025. To apply, an organization needs:

  • a signed agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency (AIA) that stays in force for the life of the certificate (under stated conditions, NB-415 lets an owner-user inspection organization fill that role);
  • a written quality management system manual, in English, that meets NBIC Part 3, Section 1.5 and describes the expected scope of work;
  • the current edition of all parts of the NBIC and a copy of the code of construction that fits the intended work;
  • a completed application on Form NB-12.

The review team is made up of a representative of the jurisdiction where the organization sits and a representative of its AIA working under the National Board's rules for commissioned inspectors. Where the jurisdiction declines, does not exist, or itself provides AIA services, the National Board represents the jurisdiction. If the company also holds or is seeking an ASME certificate, the R review can be held jointly with the ASME review; otherwise it stands alone.

The applicant demonstrates its system on current work, on a demonstration mock-up, or both. The team records what it finds on a Qualification Review Report and recommends issue, renewal or withholding of the certificate. The certificate expires three years after issue or renewal, and the renewal application is due at least six months before expiry. The jurisdiction or the National Board may audit or visit unannounced in between, and failing to follow NB-415 or the NBIC can lead to suspension and return of the stamp. Temporary locations each need National Board authorization.

Where NDE shows up on the review report

The National Board's Qualification Review Report form (NB-202) lists twenty-seven categories. Three are directly about examination: NDE, examination and tests, and calibration. Several others pull NDE in indirectly, including construction code, welding, heat treatment, field controls, the report of repair or alteration form, correction of nonconformities, and records retention.

The detail that catches people is that the team rates each category twice: once for the manual and once for implementation. Each can be marked acceptable, unacceptable, open, closed or not applicable, and manual deficiencies and implementation deficiencies go on separate attachments with the corrective action described. Your NDE program therefore has to pass on paper and then pass again when the team watches it work.

The report also records the implementation item: the vessel or part, its original code of construction, the code demonstrated, design pressure and temperature, and material and thickness. Whatever NDE you show must be the NDE that code would require for that item. A demonstration that uses a generic shop procedure, unconnected to the original code, invites an implementation deficiency. At the end the team can recommend issuing the certificate, issuing it with a follow-up by the AIA on Form NB-232, or a re-review.

NDE starts from the original code of construction

NBIC Part 3 does not carry a full set of its own acceptance standards for welds. It sends the repair organization back to the code of construction the item was built to, and it provides alternative methods for examination, testing and heat treatment when the original requirements cannot practically be met. NB-415 reinforces this by asking the organization to have the referenced standards for materials, welding and NDE the work needs, and the National Board's application page asks for a copy of the construction code appropriate to the work.

In practice, before anyone picks up a probe, the R holder has to establish what the item is:

  • the construction code and edition, from the nameplate, the data report and drawings;
  • the joint category and type of the weld being repaired, and the extent of examination used in the original design;
  • the material and thickness, which can trigger examination the original weld did not need.

Some examples show how this plays out. A through-wall repair in a longitudinal seam of a Section VIII Division 1 vessel designed with full radiography normally needs volumetric examination of the repair to the same acceptance standard. A tube butt weld replaced in a Section I boiler follows Section I rules for that joint. Excavation before a weld repair is commonly checked by MT or PT to show the defect is gone, a step that belongs in the repair procedure your Inspector accepts. An alteration that adds a nozzle brings design calculations and the NDE the construction code requires for the new joint. Where film cannot be taken or a pressure test is not practical, the Part 3 alternatives apply only with the Inspector's acceptance and any approval the jurisdiction requires, and the basis should be traceable in the job file.

Who may perform NDE on R work

Personnel qualification also follows the construction code. For items built to Section VIII Division 1 or Section I, that means radiographic and ultrasonic personnel qualified and certified to an employer's written practice based on SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, and magnetic particle and penetrant examiners who at least meet the vision and competence certification the construction code sets. Many R holders simply place every method under one written practice, which removes arguments about which route applies to which job.

Field repair work puts pressure on these records. The technician called to a plant outage carries a certification that has to be current on that night, with a near-vision check inside its annual window and a method and level that match the examination. A review team sampling a recent R-1 file will ask for that person's training, experience, examination and vision records. The Inspector may also ask for proof that the technician can actually perform and interpret the examination.

Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer certifies its own people; no course does that. Atlantis can write or revise the written practice, act as the outside Level III who prepares and grades examinations under it, and rebuild missing training records and vision records. The NBIC context for a written practice is covered in our NBIC written practice guide, and the hours planner checks training and experience totals by method.

NDE procedures for repair and field conditions

Where the construction code requires Section V examination, repair NDE still runs to a written Section V procedure that names the referencing code and the acceptance criteria. Repair work adds conditions a new-build procedure may not cover:

  • in-service surfaces with scale, coating or pitting that limit MT, PT and UT sensitivity;
  • part temperature, which bounds penetrant use and affects ultrasonic couplant and velocity;
  • access inside boilers and vessels, where geometry limits beam paths and yoke placement;
  • excavation cavities whose shape affects surface examination and later volumetric coverage;
  • examination after postweld heat treatment where the code or repair plan requires it;
  • ultrasonic examination in place of radiography, only where the construction code permits it.

Technique sheets for recurring repairs, such as tube-to-header welds, nozzle reinforcement or seam weld repairs, make field work repeatable and give the review team something concrete to sample. Atlantis writes and corrects NDE procedures and technique sheets and prepares procedure demonstrations. Method guidance for NBIC work is on our UT and PT compliance pages.

NDE subcontractors: the R holder stays responsible

Many repair organizations hire an outside NDE company, especially for radiography and phased array work. The certificate holder remains responsible for all work done under its certificate, subcontracted work included. That means the subcontractor's written practice, procedures, certifications and calibration records must be available inside the R holder's system, not just in the subcontractor's office.

The manual should describe how an NDE company is evaluated and approved, who accepts its written practice and personnel certifications, what the purchase order passes down (code of construction and edition, method, extent, acceptance standard, report content), how reports are reviewed before they reach the Inspector, and how subcontractor technicians are checked when they arrive at a field site. Our subcontractor approval audits cover each of those points.

One limit on US repair work: industrial radiography needs a 10 CFR Part 34 or Agreement State license, Atlantis holds neither, and so it shoots no radiographs for R repairs in the United States. As a Level III, Atlantis can review the film and the RT procedure your licensed contractor uses, and our report validation service checks NDE reports against procedure and acceptance criteria.

NDE records and the R form

NB-415 names two report forms: NB-66, the R-1 Report of Repair, and NB-229, the R-2 Report of Alteration. A valid certificate holder is authorized to register R reports with the National Board, and the National Board recommends its electronic data transfer system for completing and registering both. NBIC Part 3 also provides an R-3 for parts fabricated by welding and an R-4 supplementary sheet for information that does not fit on the main form.

The form summarizes the work; the NDE evidence lives in the job file that backs it. A complete NDE record for an R job identifies:

  • the item, the weld or area repaired, and the original construction code;
  • the method, procedure number and revision, and acceptance standard;
  • the technician's name, method and level, and the equipment serial number with its calibration status;
  • the results, including any rejectable indications and their re-examination after repair;
  • film or data files where the method produces them, and who holds them;
  • evidence that the Inspector reviewed the examination at the agreed point.

How long these are kept, and where, belongs in the records retention element of your manual. See NBIC examination records and records retention for the detail.

NDE deficiencies R review teams record

  • The manual says NDE follows the original code of construction but gives no step for finding out what that code requires.
  • Repair procedures name an NDE method with no procedure number or acceptance standard.
  • A subcontractor's certifications were never reviewed by the certificate holder.
  • Field technicians with lapsed near-vision checks signed recent reports.
  • The written practice cites an SNT-TC-1A edition different from the one the certifications reference.
  • Excavation examination before welding is performed but not recorded.
  • NDE equipment and reference blocks used in the field are missing from the calibration register.
  • Job files for registered R-1 forms lack the NDE reports that support them.
  • A Part 3 alternative was used without documented Inspector acceptance.

Each of these is cheaper to fix before the review than after it. Our NBIC audit preparation guide sets out the full sequence.

Engineered repairs, VR and NR certificates

Engineered repairs and alterations, a scope added under Part 3 Supplement 11, bring engineering into the decision about methods and extent of examination. The engineering basis then defines the NDE, and the NDE procedures still need to meet it.

The National Board's separate VR certificate and stamp cover repair of pressure relief valves under NB-514. That review includes witnessing the repair of sample valves, which are then tested for operation and capacity at a laboratory the National Board accepts. NDE plays a small part there; Atlantis can support the procedures and personnel records a valve shop uses for any examination, but valve testing itself is outside NDE consulting.

The NR certificate covers repair and replacement of nuclear components under NB-417. Atlantis does not support NR work, because nuclear quality assurance is outside its scope.

What Atlantis does and does not do for R certificate holders

For the R program, Atlantis reviews the NDE, examination, calibration and records elements of your manual against NBIC Part 3 and NB-415; drafts revised NDE wording for your management to approve; writes or revises the written practice, procedures and technique sheets; cleans up personnel and calibration records; audits NDE subcontractors; runs a mock review of the NDE categories on site; and helps assemble corrective action evidence after the real review. Atlantis's founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is certified ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, with 11+ years of hands-on work on projects in several countries.

The limits are just as important:

  • Atlantis is not the National Board, not a jurisdiction, not an Authorized Inspection Agency and not a commissioned Inspector. The review team decides.
  • Atlantis does not hold an R certificate. Your organization owns its quality management system and its stamp.
  • Welding procedure specifications and their qualification records belong to your organization; Atlantis does not write or qualify them. This WPS, PQR and WPQ guide explains that side.
  • Atlantis does not design repairs or alterations, and does not calculate remaining life or perform fitness-for-service assessments.

How we run an R certificate engagement, and what to send

Most of the work is remote, with a site visit for the mock review. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad and travels to repair shops and plants elsewhere.

  1. You send the documents listed below and tell us whether this is a new application, a renewal or a response to deficiencies.
  2. A Level III reviews the NDE-related manual elements and samples recent R-1 or R-2 job files end to end.
  3. We return a gap list written as the review team would write it, with the evidence needed to close each item.
  4. We draft manual text, procedures and record fixes for your approval and audit subcontractors where needed.
  5. A Level III visits for a mock review of the NDE categories, including a walk-through of the demonstration item.
  6. After the review, we help with corrective action evidence for an AIA follow-up or re-review.

What to send:

  • your quality management system manual, or its NDE, examination and test, calibration, records and subcontractor sections;
  • certificate scope (repairs, alterations, engineered work; shop or field) and the review date if known;
  • the NDE written practice and certified personnel list;
  • NDE procedures and technique sheets used on repair work;
  • the approved NDE subcontractor list and the files you hold for each;
  • two or three recent job files with their R forms and NDE reports;
  • any deficiencies from the last review or AIA audit.

If your shop also builds new equipment under an ASME certificate, our ASME audit support page covers the joint review side, and the NBIC quality manual guide covers the manual structure in more depth.

faq.q: What is an NBIC R stamp?
faq.a: It is the National Board "R" Certificate of Authorization and its symbol stamp, which authorize an organization to repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items under NBIC Part 3. The work is accepted by a commissioned Inspector and documented on an R-1 or R-2 report.

faq.q: Does NBIC Part 3 set its own NDE acceptance criteria?
faq.a: Mostly no. Part 3 points back to the original code of construction for examination requirements and acceptance standards, and provides alternative methods when those requirements cannot practically be met, used with the Inspector's acceptance and any jurisdictional approval required.

faq.q: Who conducts the R certificate review?
faq.a: Under NB-415, a team made up of a representative of the jurisdiction where your organization is located and a representative of your Authorized Inspection Agency. The National Board represents the jurisdiction where the jurisdiction declines, none exists, or it provides AIA services.

faq.q: Can our R review be combined with our ASME review?
faq.a: Yes. The National Board allows the R review to be held jointly with an ASME review, or on its own if you have no ASME certificate. See our ASME audit support page for the ASME side.

faq.q: Do our NDE technicians need SNT-TC-1A certification for R repairs?
faq.a: That depends on the code the item was built to. On items built to Section VIII Division 1 or Section I, the RT and UT people are certified under the employer's written practice, with SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 as its guideline. Putting all methods under one written practice is the simplest defensible approach.

faq.q: We subcontract all of our NDE. What will the review team expect?
faq.a: Evidence that you evaluated and approved the NDE company, accepted its written practice, procedures and certifications, flowed down the code and acceptance standard on the purchase order, and reviewed its reports before presenting them to the Inspector. You stay responsible for the subcontracted work.

faq.q: Which NDE records support an R-1 or R-2?
faq.a: The job file should hold each NDE report with the procedure and revision, acceptance standard, technician and level, equipment and calibration status, results, any re-examination after repair, and film or data where produced. See NBIC examination records.

faq.q: How long is an R certificate valid, and when do we apply to renew?
faq.a: NB-415 says the certificate expires three years after issue or renewal, and the renewal application is due at least six months before expiry. Renewals are filed through the National Board's online Business Center.

faq.q: Can Atlantis examine our repairs in the field?
faq.a: Atlantis can carry out UT, MT, PT and VT at your site, working under your subcontractor controls. Radiography is the exception in the United States, where Atlantis holds no license for it; there we can review your licensed contractor's film and RT procedure as a Level III.

faq.q: Do you help with VR or NR certificates?
faq.a: For a VR valve repair shop, Atlantis can support NDE procedures and personnel records, but the valve repair and testing program is outside our work. We do not support NR nuclear repair certificates.

faq.q: What does NBIC Part 3, Section 1.5 cover?
faq.a: NB-415 points to Part 3, Section 1.5 for the requirements of the quality management system manual an R certificate holder must maintain. Our NBIC quality manual guide covers how its NDE section is usually built.
